resources.string: Can I just crank up the bass?
Half right

Raising 200-400 Hz a little (2-3 dB), where a phone speaker still plays, makes the bass sound fuller. Raising 32, 63 or 125 Hz a lot adds almost no bass you can hear, only rattle, buzz and the phone turning itself down.
What Android phone speakers play

Phone speaker frequency response: median and 10-90% range of about 90 Android phones, and the Galaxy S26 Ultra as measured. The median phone is 10 dB under the mids near 200 Hz and about 23 dB under at 125 Hz.

Why boosting the lowest bands loses
Most of the boost is not heard. The median phone is about 23 dB under its mids at 125 Hz.
The lower the note, the further the cone moves. Bass you cannot hear drives the cone to its limit and makes rattle and buzz.
The phone amplifier turns itself down. Voices and instruments get squeezed along with the bass and the sound pumps.
What Rootnote\'s tests showed
On the S26 Ultra, 100 Hz was about 22 dB quieter than the 200 Hz region.
Cutting everything under 160 Hz made no audible difference.
An EQ with the low mids a little up and the treble a little down beat no EQ 8 to 0.
Virtual bass at +3 to +4 was cleaner than +6. Buzz appeared only when it was set too high.
Protection threshold: about -15 dBFS at 50% volume, about -27 dBFS at 80%. Loud volume takes 12 dB of headroom.
So try this
Leave the bands under 125 Hz alone, or cut them with the low cut.
Raise 200-400 Hz (low-mid lift) by 2-3 dB only.
For a heavier sound, add a little virtual bass instead of EQ.
The louder you listen, the less you raise.
About phone EQs shared online
Settings that raise 32 and 63 Hz a lot boost where most speakers cannot play. Settings that raise 250 Hz go the same way as this page.
Sources: difference transfer of one reviewer\'s measurements (docs/SPEAKER_ESTIMATES.md), Moliner et al. 2020 (DAFx), TI TAS2563 datasheet, Rootnote measurements and blind listening.
